0.body: Maestro runs a program many times on a group of shared machines and keeps what each run produces. You keep the program in a git repository with a Dockerfile. Maestro clones the repository, builds a container image from it, and starts one container for each set of parameters you list. A hundred seeds become a hundred containers. Each container gets the cores and memory it asked for, on whichever machine has room for it first. When a container ends, Maestro keeps what it printed and the files it wrote. You download them, or read them in your browser. The machines are shared, so everyone's containers wait in one queue. Users take turns in it, and an administrator chooses the rules that decide whose container starts next.

0.title: What Maestro is

100.body: Maestro copies each path in outputs out of the container. A directory comes with everything in it. Only regular files and directories are kept, so symbolic links, devices and similar entries are skipped. An output the program didn't write is listed as missing, as in out.txt (missing) under FILES in maestro runs show. With outputs_layout = "shared" , the outputs of every line go into one tree for the run, under shared/. When two lines write the same path, the one Maestro collects last overwrites the other.

105.body: The sidebar has My runs, Queue and Usage. Administrators also get All users and the admin pages: Machines, Groups and Settings. On a narrow screen the sidebar shrinks to a rail of icons. At the foot of the sidebar are the account you signed in with, Sign out, and the theme toggle. The page follows your system's light or dark theme until you use the toggle, and the browser then remembers your choice. The address bar always holds the page you are on. You can send someone a link to a run, a line or a file, and it opens for anyone allowed to see it.
105.title: The sidebar

106.body: My runs lists your runs, newest first. You can narrow the list to active or finished runs, and search it by run number or repository. Administrators find everyone's runs under All users. Opening a run shows its lines, with the cores and memory each one asked for. You can sort them by line number, arguments, cores, memory, machine or number of files kept. Click a column's heading to sort by it, and click again to reverse the order. The Status column works differently. Each click moves the next status to the top, starting with the ones that are over (cancelled, then error, then failed) and going round to queued. The page draws a line that ended in error in amber and says what happened, because the cause was on the server's side and the line is worth running again. A failed line ran, and its program exited with an error. How a line ends lists every status. Cancelling a run cancels the lines that hadn't ended. A line that had already ended keeps its status.
106.title: My runs

107.body: A line's page opens on its files. The Details button shows everything the line's container ran with: its cores and memory its command its environment, with the run's env first and then the MAESTRO_ variables the files kept from it the name of its container, its image and the commit the image was built from when it was queued, assigned, started and finished, and how long it waited and ran The page shows files as folders. Paths that share a prefix go under one folder, and a chain of folders that each hold only the next one shows as a single row, such as results/7/1/0.01_0.01. Click a folder to fold it. A run whose outputs are shared also has a page for the whole tree, with every line's files merged and each file marked with the line that wrote it.
107.title: A line

108.body: Click a file or one of a line's two logs to open it in a pane beside the list. You can also open it in its own tab or download it. While a line runs, the page reads its logs again every 5 seconds. A line, or a whole run, downloads as a zip laid out the way maestro runs get leaves it. The page shows text, PDFs and images (png, jpeg, gif and webp). Any other file can only be downloaded. Text is highlighted by its extension. Python, JSON, TOML, YAML, shell, C and C++, Go, Rust, Julia, R, SQL, Markdown, HTML and XML are among the languages it knows. Three kinds of file are drawn, with the source one click away: File Shown as CSV A table SVG An image. None of its scripts run. HTML The page itself, in a sandbox The sandbox runs the HTML page's scripts, so a chart in it draws. It gives the page an origin of its own, so the page can't read your session, call the server as you, or navigate the Maestro page away. Any preview can go full screen. A drawn file opened in its own tab is drawn the same way, sandbox included. A program that writes its results as an HTML chart, an SVG or a CSV can therefore be read on the page without a download.
108.title: Files

115.body: The server reads a machine by running one small shell script over SSH. The script reads /proc and df, and nvidia-smi when the machine has it. The server asks Podman for the containers' usage. GPUs are read only when they are NVIDIA's and the machine runs Linux. Some machines let the server's SSH user reach the Podman socket and nothing else. Such a machine still appears with its containers, and says why it has no other numbers. The server keeps each reading for 2 seconds and shares it among everyone watching. However many maestro top windows are open, each machine gets one SSH connection every couple of seconds. The cores lines take and the lines waiting come from the server's own records, so they are always current.

120.body: orq makes every decision in Maestro. It signs people in through the lab's identity provider, clones repositories with the forge tokens the CLI sends it, and builds images with its own Podman. It records every build, run and line in a SQLite database. orq also runs the scheduler. The scheduler is a loop that picks which waiting line goes to which machine, copies images to the machines, starts containers, and collects what they leave. Because everything about a run is in the database, orq can restart in the middle of one and continue from where it stopped.
120.title: orq, the server

121.body: The view is the Maestro page, a web page served from the same host as orq. It shows your runs and their files, the queue, your usage, and the admin pages. It keeps no state of its own and asks orq for everything it shows.
121.title: The view

122.body: The CLI is the maestro command, which does everything from a terminal. On your computer it keeps the server's address, your Maestro key and your forge tokens.
122.title: The CLI

123.body: A machine is a computer with Podman and an SSH server. It needs no Maestro software. orq connects to each machine over SSH and talks to the machine's Podman socket through that connection. It copies images to the machine, starts containers, reads how loaded the machine is, and takes the logs and outputs back when a container ends. orq removes a container once it has the container's logs and outputs. The image stays on the machine, so the next run of the same build starts without copying it again.
123.title: The machines

A line in the dispatcher queue is still queued. Being a head isn't a status: the scheduler works your head out again on every pass.

127.body: maestro run puts every line of the run in your user queue. The user policy puts your queued lines in an order, and the first of them is your head. By default it is the oldest run first, line by line. With lcfs or pq, a line you queue later can take your head's place. A line that no machine could hold, even an empty one, is never your head. It waits without holding back your other lines.
127.breadcrumbs: The queue » The user queue: your head
127.title: The user queue: your head

128.body: flowchart LR subgraph lab["group lab"] a["Ada's queue"] --> ah(("Ada's head")) b["Bo's queue"] --> bh(("Bo's head")) end subgraph physics["group physics"] c["Cy's queue"] --> ch(("Cy's head")) end ah --> dl["lab's dispatcher queue"] bh --> dl ch --> dp["physics' dispatcher queue"] dl -- "in turn" --> q1["Q1's queue"] dp -- "in turn" --> q1 dl -- "in turn" --> q2["Q2's queue"] dp -- "in turn" --> q2 Each group has a dispatcher queue, made of the heads of its users and nothing else. It has no size of its own: it holds one line for each user who has lines waiting. Groups take turns at the machines, one line a turn. In its turn, a group's dispatcher policy picks one of its heads and gives it to a machine. The machine has to be one the line may run on, by its machines , and it has to have room in its queue. Only three lines wait on each machine by default. When several machines qualify, the scheduler draws one at random. A group with no head that can go anywhere passes its turn. Your administrator may set a ceiling on the cores each user holds, user_max_cpus. Your lines assigned, starting and running count toward it, and your queued lines don't. While your head's cores, added to theirs, would be over the ceiling, your head isn't a candidate. It stays in the dispatcher queue, and the heads of other users go as usual. It goes once enough of your lines end. Once your head is given a machine, your next line is your head. The dispatcher policy can be as simple as the oldest head, or it can weigh how much of the machines each user already holds. While the line waits on the machine, the server copies the line's image there if the machine doesn't have it yet.
128.breadcrumbs: The queue » The dispatcher queue: from queued to assigned
128.title: The dispatcher queue: from queued to assigned

129.body: A machine starts a waiting line when the line's cores and memory fit in what the machine has free. The machine policy picks which of the lines waiting on the machine starts first.

137.body: Most machine policies, such as fifo-skip and best-fit, choose among the lines that fit in the free space now, so smaller lines go around a large one that doesn't fit yet. 138.body: Ask for the cores and memory the program needs and no more. A line starts only where its cpus and memory fit, so a smaller line fits on more machines and sooner. Leave machines out unless the program needs particular hardware. Keep the image small. The first line of a build on each machine waits while the image is copied.

139.body: A machine the server can't reach, over SSH or at its Podman socket, gets no new lines. The lines that were waiting on it, or about to start there, go back to queued, in their place in their user's queue, so another machine can take them. They don't end in an error. The server tries the machine again every 30 seconds. Lines already running on the machine are left alone. The server checks on them when the machine is back.

142.body: Setting The choice it makes Queue user Which of one user's queued lines is that user's head User queue dispatcher Which of a group's heads goes to a machine in the group's turn Dispatcher queue machine Which of the lines waiting on a machine starts Machine queue All three are fifo until an administrator changes them. 142.title: The three policies

143.body: The user and dispatcher policies choose before a line is on a machine. At that point there is no free space to fit the line into, so these policies only put lines in an order. Policy Serves first fifo The oldest lcfs The newest siro One at random. The same seed gives the same choices. pq The one with the highest score . Among equal scores, the oldest. The machine policy can be any of those four, and it also has four that look at the machine's free cores and memory. Policy Serves first, among the lines that fit now fifo-skip The oldest best-fit The one that leaves the least free weighted-best-fit As best-fit, with the time a line has waited counting in its favour by ω3. A line that fits badly still starts eventually. tetris The one whose cores and memory are most like what the machine has free, so that less of either is stranded (Grandl et al., 2014) On a machine, fifo and lcfs are strict. They start their first choice if it fits, and start nothing while it doesn't. siro and pq choose among the lines that fit now, as the four policies in the second table do.
143.breadcrumbs: Policies and the score » What a policy can be
143.title: What a policy can be

144.body: pq gives every candidate line a score and serves the highest. s = ω1·cores + ω2·memory + ω3·waiting + ω4·share Term What it is cores The line's cpus, as a fraction of the cores all machines have for lines, summed memory The line's memory, as a fraction of the memory all machines have for lines, summed waiting The time since the line's run was queued, divided by the horizon. The horizon is an hour unless horizon_minutes says otherwise. share The user's share of the machines, as a fraction of every user's share added together The cores and memory are fractions of all the machines together, so they are small when there are many machines. ω1 and ω2 then need to be larger to weigh as much as waiting and share do. An administrator sets the four weights, and a weight can be negative. Weight Setting Effect ω1 cpu_weight Below 0, lines that ask for few cores go first. ω2 memory_weight Below 0, lines that ask for little memory go first. ω3 aging_weight Above 0, a line's score grows while it waits, so no line waits forever. ω4 share_weight Below 0, a user who holds less of the machines goes first.
144.breadcrumbs: Policies and the score » The score
144.title: The score

145.body: Take a lab whose machines have 32 cores for lines in all, with dispatcher = pq and these weights: ω1 = −0.4, ω2 = 0, ω3 = 0.5 and ω4 = −1. The horizon is an hour. Two users of a group each have a head. Ada's line Bo's line Cores asked for 4, so cores = 0.125 8, so cores = 0.25 Run queued 30 minutes ago, so waiting = 0.5 6 minutes ago, so waiting = 0.1 User's share 0.75 0.25 ω1·cores −0.05 −0.10 ω3·waiting +0.25 +0.05 ω4·share −0.75 −0.25 Score −0.55 −0.30 Bo's line has the higher score, so it goes to a machine first. Ada's line has waited longer and is smaller, but Ada already holds three times what Bo holds, and with these weights the share outweighs the rest. Giving Bo's line a machine raises Bo's share, because an assigned line counts as held. The scheduler works the shares out again before the next turn.

145.title: A worked example

146.body: The share setting chooses how a user's share is measured. Measure A user's share is drf The dominant share now. Take the cores the user's lines hold as a fraction of the cores the machines have for lines, and the same for memory. The share is the larger of the two fractions (Ghodsi et al., 2011). weighted-drf As drf, with each fraction divided by the user's weight for that resource. An administrator sets the weights for each user, and a user without any has 1 for both. asset The two fractions added together. It is there for comparison only, because it lacks the sharing-incentive property that drf has. decay The dominant share of what the user's lines have used in the past. Usage counts half as much after each half-life, which is a week unless half_life_hours says otherwise. Slurm's fair-share works this way. For drf, weighted-drf and asset, the lines a user holds are those that are assigned, starting or running. Suppose the machines of the lab in the example have 32 cores and 96 GB for lines in total, and the measure is drf. Ada's lines hold 12 cores and 16 GB. That is 0.375 of the cores and 0.167 of the memory, so her dominant share is 0.375. Bo's lines hold 3 cores and 12 GB, which is 0.094 and 0.125, so his is 0.125. The score uses each as a fraction of the two together, which gives 0.75 for Ada and 0.25 for Bo. With dispatcher = pq, share = drf and ω4 = −1, the queue is the classic fair queue of DRF, in which the user who holds the least goes next.

154.body:
orq is reached through the reverse proxy and nothing else. The compose file publishes its port 3005 on 127.0.0.1, so only the host itself reaches it. A reverse proxy in a container of its own reaches the host through Podman's bridge, at host.containers.internal, and a port published on 127.0.0.1 may not answer there. Try it on your host. If the proxy can't reach orq, do one of two things: Set ORQ_BIND in .env to an address of the host that the proxy reaches and other hosts don't. Put the proxy and orq on one Podman network, have the proxy reach orq by its name, and remove the ports entry from the compose file. The host also needs a firewall that lets in SSH and the ports the reverse proxy listens on, usually 80 and 443, and nothing else. A port that rootful Docker or Podman publishes can get past some firewalls' rules, so publish orq on 127.0.0.1 even behind one. With firewalld: firewall-cmd --permanent --add-service=http --add-service=https
firewall-cmd --permanent --list-services # remove any other with --remove-service
firewall-cmd --reload

155.body: Redis holds the sessions of the Maestro page, so whoever can write to it can make a session and sign in as anyone, administrators included. Builds run on the same host and may reach it. Hold it to two rules: Give it a password. Make one with openssl rand -hex 32, which needs no escaping in a URL. Start Redis with --requirepass <password>, or put requirepass <password> in its redis.conf. Then set REDIS_URL=redis://:<password>@host:port/db in .env. Unless MODE=dev, orq logs a warning at start while REDIS_URL has no password. Don't publish its port beyond the host. Other hosts must not reach it. A Redis that other services share gets the same care from each of them. Any one of them that publishes it, or lets its own users reach it, opens Maestro's sessions too. When the Redis belongs to another compose project, its owner sets the password there, and you then set it in REDIS_URL.

159.body: Register Maestro with your provider as a confidential client that uses the authorization code flow. The redirect URI is <orq>/api/auth/callback. Then configure orq with these variables: Variable Default Meaning OIDC_ISSUER required The issuer URL. It must serve /.well-known/openid-configuration. OIDC_CLIENT_ID required OIDC_CLIENT_SECRET required OIDC_REDIRECT_URL required <orq>/api/auth/callback, as registered with the provider OIDC_SCOPES openid email profile Separated by spaces OIDC_ROLES_CLAIM roles The ID token claim that holds the user's roles, as a string or a list. Some providers use groups. OIDC_ALLOWED_ROLES empty Separated by commas. When empty, anyone the provider authenticates can sign in. VIEW_URL The first of ALLOWED_ORIGINS Where the Maestro page is served. Sign-ins return there. REDIS_URL required redis://[:password@]host:port/db of the Redis, Valkey or KeyDB that keeps sessions SESSION_TTL 12h How long a Maestro session lasts KEY_TTL 2160h (90 days) How long a Maestro key works after it was issued. 0 means keys never expire. COOKIE_SECURE true, or false with MODE=dev Set it to false only when you serve over plain http. The page needs VITE_ORQ_URL, and optionally VITE_IDP_NAME for the label of the sign-in button.

162.body: Signing out of Maestro ends the Maestro session and leaves the user signed in at the provider. Signing out at the provider leaves an open Maestro session running until it expires. The CLI doesn't use sessions. maestro login has the user approve a code on the page, and orq then gives the CLI a Maestro key of its own. orq stores only the key's hash. A key expires KEY_TTL after it was issued, 90 days by default. A key can be revoked three ways. Its owner revokes it with maestro keys rm, maestro logout revokes the key it holds, and an administrator revokes every key of a user with Revoke keys in Admin › Groups. A revoked key stops working at once. Whether a user is an administrator is read from their row in users on every request. That row is as fresh as their last sign-in on the page. A user removed at the identity provider keeps a working key for at most KEY_TTL, so revoke their keys when you remove them.

163.body: A machine is a host whose Podman runs users' containers. orq connects to it over SSH and talks to the Podman socket through that connection. The machine needs an SSH server and Podman's API socket, and no Maestro software.

164.body:
Run this on the machine, as the user the containers will run as: systemctl --user enable --now podman.socket
loginctl enable-linger "$USER" # keep the socket up without a session
ls /run/user/$(id -u)/podman/podman.sock Make an SSH key pair without a passphrase for orq, and add the public key to that user's ~/.ssh/authorized_keys. Let the user run commands over SSH. orq reads how loaded a machine is with a small shell script that uses /proc, df and nvidia-smi. A user who may only reach the socket still runs lines, but maestro top then shows the machine's containers and nothing else.

165.body:
Some machines can't limit how much CPU a container uses. This happens with rootless Podman when the user's systemd doesn't pass down the cpu cgroup controller, which is the default on Ubuntu 22.04. On such a machine lines still count their cpus toward the machine's capacity, but a line that uses more cores gets them and slows the others down. To get the limit, delegate the controllers to users once: sudo mkdir -p /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d
printf '[Service]\nDelegate=cpu cpuset io memory pids\n' | sudo tee /etc/systemd/system/user@.service.d/delegate.conf
sudo systemctl daemon-reload Then have the Podman user sign out of every session, or restart the machine, so that the user's systemd starts again with the new setting. podman info should now list cpu under cgroupControllers.

It saves the machine only if that works, and it refuses a reserve that would leave nothing for lines. orq asks again every time it checks the machine, so it notices when a machine gains or loses cores or memory.

FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim # Relative `outputs` are looked for here.
WORKDIR /work COPY requirements.txt /app/requirements.txt
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r /app/requirements.txt
COPY . /app # Your program. Each line of `parameters` replaces CMD and reaches it as
# arguments; -u prints as it goes, so logs can be followed.
ENTRYPOINT ["python", "-u", "/app/main.py"] # Used when maestro.toml has no lines.
CMD ["-t", "1", "out.txt"] Three of its instructions decide how Maestro runs the image. Instruction What Maestro does with it ENTRYPOINT The program every container starts. Maestro never changes it. CMD The arguments the program gets when a run supplies none. A line of parameters replaces it. WORKDIR The directory the program starts in. A relative path among the files to keep is looked for here. So the template's containers run python -u /app/main.py followed by either a line of parameters or, when there are none, -t 1 out.txt. Write ENTRYPOINT as a list, as above. Written as plain text (ENTRYPOINT python /app/main.py), it runs through a shell that drops the arguments, and every line would run the program with none. The rest of the Dockerfile is yours. Any language works, because Maestro only starts the container. A compiled program can be built in one stage and copied into a small image: FROM docker.io/library/gcc:14 AS build
WORKDIR /src
COPY . .
RUN make solver FROM docker.io/library/debian:bookworm-slim
WORKDIR /work
COPY --from=build /src/solver /usr/local/bin/solver
ENTRYPOINT ["solver"]
CMD ["--help"]

173.body: orq sweeps each machine when it starts, every 10 minutes, and whenever an image is removed. orq labels everything it creates with maestro.orq, set to a name it gave itself the first time it started. Its images also carry their build, and its containers carry their run and line. The sweep removes two things: a container of orq's own that no line has on that machine, and an image of orq's own that orq no longer has and no line needs there. The sweep touches nothing else on the machine. The machine's own images and containers stay, and so do those of another orq that uses the same machine. Images and containers that an orq made before it labelled what it made have no maestro.orq label. Every orq takes them for its own, as it did then.

174.body: A machine orq can't reach gets no new lines. The lines waiting on it, or about to start there, go back to queued so another machine can take them. orq tries the machine again every 30 seconds. Lines already running on it are left alone. orq doesn't keep SSH connections open. The runner, a check of the machine, and maestro top each open their own. maestro top opens one every couple of seconds while someone is watching.

In the machine's form, set the host to the Access hostname, such as q1-ssh.example.com, and set the proxy command to: cloudflared access ssh --hostname %h orq replaces %h, %p and %r with the host, the port and the user, and %% with a %. cloudflared is included in orq's image. A repository with a Dockerfile and no maestro.toml builds and runs. The build log says what its runs will do: No maestro.toml. Runs will use the default: 1 line running the image's own command on any machine, with 1 core and 512 MB each, keeping only its logs. A run of that build is one line: Run 32 of ada/maestro-template@main (build #13): succeeded, on any machine
1 line(s): 1 succeeded LINE PARAMETERS MACHINE STATUS FILES
1 (image's command) Q1 succeeded - That is one container, started with the image's own CMD, with 1 core and 512 MB, on any machine. Maestro keeps what it printed and no files, so the out.txt the program wrote is gone with the container. This is enough to run one long job on the lab's machines. 185.body: Label Setting Default Images per user images_per_user 10, and at most 1000 Cores per user user_max_cpus 0, which means no ceiling Lowering "Images per user" removes nobody's images at that moment. A user who is over the new number loses images at their next build, which removes as many of the ones they ran least recently as it takes to make room. The build is refused only when runs are still using all the images that are left. "Cores per user" is a ceiling on the cores each user holds. A user's lines assigned, starting and running count toward it, and their queued lines don't. In a group's turn, a user's head isn't a candidate while its cores, added to those, would be over the ceiling. The heads of other users go as usual. Lowering it stops no line. It only holds back a user's next lines until enough of theirs end. A line that asks for more cores than the ceiling never starts, and while it is its user's head, their lines behind it wait too. maestro queue tells a user when their next line waits for the ceiling.

186.body: maestro settings prints the saved settings for any user, and maestro queue ends with a one-line summary of them. Each line records the settings it was assigned under and the group its user was in. An export that spans a change of settings therefore still says which settings served which line. Settings saved before orq had three queues had a select policy, which chose among a group's users. orq reads it as the dispatcher policy, so a pq there stays pq. Their allocate and staged_capacity no longer set anything. If orq can't read the saved settings after an upgrade, it falls back to FIFO in every queue so that lines keep starting, and its log says why. Save the settings again to fix it.

188.body: Every user is in one group, and groups take turns at the machines. Each group has a dispatcher queue of its own, made of its users' heads, so a group with many users can't crowd out a group with few. A new Maestro has one group, the default group, and everyone is in it. New users start there. It stays the only group until an administrator makes more.
188.title: Groups

189.body: Admin › Groups on the Maestro page lists the groups and their members. "New group" creates a group, and Rename changes a group's name. "Add member" moves a user into a group. A user is in one group at a time, so this takes the user out of the group they were in. The ✕ beside a member sends that user back to the default group. Remove deletes a group and sends its users back to the default group. The default group itself can't be removed. Under the groups, "Maestro keys" lists every user. "Revoke keys" revokes all of a user's Maestro keys after it asks. Moving a user affects the lines assigned from then on. Their queued lines wait in the new group's dispatcher queue. Lines already assigned keep the group they were assigned in.
189.title: Managing groups

19.body: Maestro builds the Containerfile at the root of the repository, or else the Dockerfile there. To build from a file somewhere else, name it in maestro.toml with dockerfile . The root of the repository is the build's context wherever the Dockerfile is, so the paths in COPY start at the root. A repository with neither file doesn't reach the server. maestro build stops and says that it has no Dockerfile.
19.breadcrumbs: The minimum: a Dockerfile » Where Maestro looks for the Dockerfile
19.title: Where Maestro looks for the Dockerfile

190.body: Inside a group, the dispatcher policy chooses whose head goes to a machine next. Between groups no policy chooses. The groups take turns, one line a turn. The queue describes a turn. maestro queue shows each user their group: how many of its lines are queued, how many of those are heads in its dispatcher queue, and how many are assigned. Each line records the group its user was in when the line was assigned. maestro export writes it, so moving a user later doesn't change what the export says about earlier lines.
190.breadcrumbs: Groups » How groups affect the queue
190.title: How groups affect the queue

191.body:
sim is a program in the maestro-orq repository. It runs orq's own scheduler over a workload on a simulated clock, so you can compare policies without using the machines. It also measures how lines were served, whether they came from a simulation or from a real Maestro. It can replay the lines of a real week, to check how closely the simulator follows your machines. cd maestro-orq
go run ./cmd/sim generate -users 4 -groups 2 -hours 8 > workload.csv
go run ./cmd/sim run -machines Q1:32:65536:2:4096 -config drf.json < workload.csv > lines.csv
go run ./cmd/sim evaluate -cpus 30 -memory 61440 -lambda-j 1h -lambda-o 1h < lines.csv
191.breadcrumbs: Comparing policies offline » Comparing policies offline
191.title: Comparing policies offline

192.body: sim generate writes a workload: runs of lines that users submit over a number of hours. The group column puts each user in a group. A workload without that column has every user in group 1.
192.title: A workload

193.body: -machines takes a list separated by commas. Each machine is written name:cpus:memory[:reserve_cpus:reserve_memory][@speed], with memory in MB. Example Meaning Q1:32:65536:2:4096 32 cores and 64 GB, with 2 cores and 4 GB kept back Q2:8:16384@1.5 8 cores and 16 GB. Lines run 1.5 times as fast on it. With @speed, how long a line runs depends on the machine it lands on.
193.title: The machines

194.body: -config names a JSON file with the scheduler's settings, in the form GET /api/settings returns them under scheduler. This one is DRF: {"dispatcher": "pq", "share_weight": -1} Without -config, every queue is FIFO. The names are the settings of Policies and the score : Kind Names Policies user, dispatcher, machine Score cpu_weight, memory_weight, aging_weight, share_weight, horizon_minutes Share share, half_life_hours The machine queue and the draw depth, seed -user-max-cpus is the ceiling on the cores each user holds, as "Cores per user" sets it on the Maestro page. It is 0, no ceiling, by default. sim run, sim replay and sim grid all take it, and sim grid takes one value. A file from before the three queues still works. Its select is read as dispatcher, and its allocate and staged_capacity are ignored. A simulated line starts the moment it is chosen. A real line first waits for its image to be copied and its container to be created, which the simulation leaves out.
194.breadcrumbs: Comparing policies offline » The scheduler's settings
194.title: The scheduler's settings

195.body: sim evaluate reads lines from sim run or from maestro export and reports: the mean wait, and how much of it was spent queued and assigned the mean time in the system the mean bounded slowdown the utilization of cores and of memory Jain's index of the users' slowdowns the objective Z = F + λ_J·Φ_J + λ_O·Φ_O An export from before the three queues has a staged column, which sim evaluate skips. Its lines' time queued then runs to when they were assigned. The objective has three parts. Part What it is F The mean time from a run's submission to the end of its last line Φ_J The gap between the largest and the smallest dominant share, among users who have unfinished lines, averaged over time Φ_O The fraction of the machines that is idle while some line waits, averaged over time -lambda-j and -lambda-o say how much time one whole unit of Φ_J and of Φ_O is worth. The Usage page on the Maestro page measures a real period the same way, under "Lines over a period". It uses what the machines have for lines at the moment you ask.
195.title: Measuring

196.body:
sim compare measures two files of lines, as sim evaluate does, and prints them side by side. The last column is the second file's value less the first's. go run ./cmd/sim compare -cpus 30 -memory 61440 week.csv replayed.csv MEASURE week.csv replayed.csv DIFFERENCE
lines 296 296 0
wq 13535.196 13125.912 -409.284
queued 12677.507 12269.348 -408.159
... It takes the same flags as sim evaluate. Times are in seconds. The utilizations, Φ_J and Φ_O are fractions between 0 and 1.
196.breadcrumbs: Comparing policies offline » Comparing two files of lines
196.title: Comparing two files of lines

197.body: sim grid runs one workload under many settings and writes a CSV with one row for each. You give it lists, separated by commas, and it runs every combination of them: Flag A list of -user user queue policies -dispatcher dispatcher queue policies -machine machine queue policies -share share measures -seed seeds A list you leave out keeps the value in the -config file. It also takes -machines, -config, -tick and -user-max-cpus as sim run does, and -theta, -lambda-j and -lambda-o as sim evaluate does. go run ./cmd/sim grid -machines Q1:32:65536:2:4096 -config base.json \ -dispatcher fifo,pq -share drf,decay -seed 1,2,3,4,5 < workload.csv > grid.csv This runs 2 × 2 × 5 = 20 simulations. Each row starts with the settings user, dispatcher, machine, share and seed. Every measure sim compare names follows, under the same name. The cores and memory that utilization is measured against are what the machines have for lines. On the same commit, the same arguments write the same file, byte for byte. The simulations run at once, but the rows always come in the same order: the user policy changes slowest and the seed fastest.
197.breadcrumbs: Comparing policies offline » Running every combination
197.title: Running every combination

198.body:
sim replay reads an export and runs its lines again. Each line that ran becomes a line of the workload, with its user, group, cores and memory. It arrives when it was submitted, and it runs as long as it ran, from started to finished. A line that never ran is left out, and sim replay says how many it left out. It takes the same flags as sim run. To see how closely the simulator follows your machines: Pick a week in which nobody changed the scheduler's settings. The policy_set column of the export says which settings each line was assigned under, so every line of the week should have the same one. Export the week: maestro export --all --since 2026-11-02 --until 2026-11-09 -o week.csv Write the machines as they were that week, with what each kept back, for -machines. Save the scheduler's settings from that week as a JSON file for -config, and give its cores per user to -user-max-cpus. Replay the week, and compare the replay with what happened: go run ./cmd/sim replay -machines Q1:32:65536:2:4096,Q2:32:65536:2:4096 -config week.json < week.csv > replayed.csv
go run ./cmd/sim compare -cpus 60 -memory 122880 week.csv replayed.csv The smaller the differences, the better the simulator predicts your machines. Some differences come from what the simulation leaves out: A real line waits for its image to be copied and its container to be created before it starts. A simulated line starts at once. The export doesn't say which machines a line was allowed to use, so the replay lets each line use any machine. A machine that was down for part of the week is up for all of it in the replay. siro and the choice among machines with room draw at random. The seed repeats the simulation's draws, but not the real cluster's. Two runs of one user submitted within the same second become one run. That changes only F, which is measured over runs. With @speed, sim replay multiplies a line's time by the speed of the machine it ran on, so that the line runs as long again on that machine. Maestro's tests check that a simulation's own lines, replayed on the same machines with the same settings and seed, give every line the same wait. A difference between a replay and a real week is something the simulator doesn't model.
198.breadcrumbs: Comparing policies offline » Checking the simulator against a real week
198.title: Checking the simulator against a real week

199.body: orq keeps four kinds of data: its record of builds and runs in SQLite, the files runs leave, the images, and short-lived answers in Redis.

2.body: Each chapter adds one thing to what the previous one showed. The quickstart builds and runs a ready-made template, so you see a whole run before you learn its parts. The minimum: a Dockerfile starts from the least a repository needs. The next chapters add maestro.toml , which runs the image many times, and a Python script that computes the parameters. Working with Maestro covers the commands and the web page you use every day, from builds to downloaded results. How Maestro works explains the programs Maestro is made of, the queue, and the score that orders it. Running a Maestro is for administrators. It covers deploying the server, adding machines and choosing the queue's policies. The reference lists every command , every maestro.toml key and every environment variable , and has a troubleshooting page and a glossary . If you want results and nothing more, read as far as the generator chapter.

20.body: COPY . /app copies the repository into the image, except what .dockerignore lists. The template's .dockerignore leaves out caches, the README, and also maestro.toml and genvrs.py. Maestro reads those two from the repository when it builds. The program never needs them. Maestro's clone has no .git directory. Git keeps the forge token there, and the token would end up in the image. A RUN git rev-parse HEAD in a Dockerfile therefore fails. The Maestro page shows which commit a line's image was built from. A smaller image starts sooner. The first time a line runs on a machine, Maestro copies the image there, and the line waits for the copy.

20.title: What goes into the image

200.body: orq keeps everything about builds, runs and lines in its database, which lets it restart in the middle of a run. When it comes back: it starts again the lines it was about to start it picks up the containers it had started, where they are it collects the containers that finished while it was down, as if it had been running A build that orq was making when it stopped is marked failed, so it doesn't count against the user's image limit. orq removes any image that build left behind.
200.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » The record, in SQLite
200.title: The record, in SQLite

201.body: The database is MAESTRO_ORQ_DB, which the compose file puts at /data/maestro-orq.db in the maestro-orq-data volume. When DB_BACKUP_DIR is set, orq backs the database up there on its own. It writes the first copy a minute after it starts, and another every 24 hours after that. Each copy is named after the day it was made, in UTC, such as maestro-orq-2026-11-16.db, and a second copy on the same day replaces the first. orq writes it with SQLite's VACUUM INTO, which is safe while orq runs. It keeps the 7 newest copies and removes the older ones. DB_BACKUPS_KEPT changes the number, and 0 keeps every copy. The compose file sets DB_BACKUP_DIR to /backups, in the maestro-orq-backups volume. That volume is on the same server as the database, so copy its files off the server too. You can also back the database up yourself. orq opens the database in WAL mode, so the latest writes sit in maestro-orq.db-wal beside it until SQLite moves them into the database. A copy of maestro-orq.db alone can miss them. Back the database up in one of two ways: While orq runs, use SQLite's own backup, which reads both files consistently: sqlite3 maestro-orq.db ".backup maestro-orq-backup.db". Stop orq, then copy maestro-orq.db together with maestro-orq.db-wal and maestro-orq.db-shm, if they are there.
201.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Backing up the database
201.title: Backing up the database

202.body: Stop orq: podman compose stop orq Put the database aside with its -wal and -shm files, and copy the backup in its place. Leave no -wal file of the old database beside the copy, because SQLite would read it as part of the copy. podman compose run --rm --entrypoint sh orq -c ' mkdir -p /data/before-restore && mv /data/maestro-orq.db* /data/before-restore/ && cp /backups/maestro-orq-2026-11-16.db /data/maestro-orq.db' Start orq: podman compose start orq If the copy was made by an older orq, orq brings the database up to date as it starts, as it does after an update. The copy holds the database and nothing else. The logs and outputs of runs aren't in it, and a restore leaves /maestro/data as it is. A restore loses everything orq wrote to the database after the copy was made: Runs started after the copy aren't in it, and orq doesn't list them. Their files stay in /maestro/data and count toward their owners' USER_DATA_MAX_GB. orq gives their numbers to the next runs. Once orq is back, maestro runs --all shows the newest run it knows. Move the directories of runs numbered above it, /maestro/data/<user>/<run>, out of /maestro/data before new runs take those numbers. A line that was running when the copy was made, and ended after, is ended as error, with "the container disappeared from ". Its container was removed after orq collected it, so orq can't collect it again. A run deleted after the copy is listed again, without its files. A line that was waiting when the copy was made starts again, even if it ran after the copy. Builds, machines, settings, groups and Maestro keys changed after the copy go back to what they were. A key issued after the copy stops working, and a key revoked after it works again.
202.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Restoring a backup
202.title: Restoring a backup

203.body: orq keeps the logs and outputs of runs under DATA_DIR, which is /maestro/data by default, as <user>/<run>/<line>/<file>. Each line keeps at most RUN_OUTPUT_MAX_MB of logs and outputs, 1024 by default. The files stay until someone deletes the run. orq deletes none of them on its own, so size the volume for that, and ask users to remove the runs they no longer need with maestro runs rm. USER_DATA_MAX_GB limits what all of a user's runs keep, and is off by default. orq adds up the user's files when they start a run. Once they keep that much or more, it refuses the run with "your runs keep 52 GB of the 50 GB allowed; delete one with maestro runs rm <run>". orq checks only when a run starts, so a run already started can take the user past the limit, by at most RUN_OUTPUT_MAX_MB for each of its lines.
203.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Files, in /maestro/data
203.title: Files, in /maestro/data

204.body: Each user keeps at most 10 built images. Admin › Settings changes the number. A build that would exceed it removes the image the user ran least recently, skipping any image a run is still using. The image goes from orq's Podman and from the machines. The record of its build, the runs of that build and their files are all kept.
204.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Images
204.title: Images

205.body: Lists are requested often, mostly by tab completion, so orq answers the slow ones from Redis. Redis holds no record that exists nowhere else. If you empty it, orq reads each answer again the next time it is asked. Sessions of the Maestro page are in Redis too, so emptying it signs everyone out of the page. The CLI stays signed in, because its keys are in the database. Answer Kept for Dropped sooner when A user's images (maestro builds, completing maestro run) 60 s A build of theirs ends, or one of their images is removed Runs (maestro runs, completing a run, the page) 2 s Their owner or an administrator starts, cancels or deletes one A machine's status 10 min. An answer older than 30 s, or 10 s if the machine was unreachable, triggers a new check in the background. The machine is edited A machine's load (maestro top) 2 s In practice, what a user does shows at once, and what the runner does to a run, such as a line starting or ending, shows within 2 seconds. An image removed from Podman by hand, without orq knowing, can stay listed for up to a minute. The list of builds is one fast query and isn't cached. The CLI caches nothing either, so each tab completion costs one request to orq.
205.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » Short-lived answers, in Redis
205.title: Short-lived answers, in Redis

206.body: orq removes a container once it has the container's logs and outputs. An image stays on a machine, so the next run of its build starts without a copy. It goes when orq removes the image itself, either to make room for a newer build or because of maestro builds rm. orq's sweep then removes it from every machine where no line needs it. Adding machines describes the sweep.
206.breadcrumbs: What orq keeps, and for how long » On the machines
206.title: On the machines

207.body: Written by the CLI itself when the book is built, so it says what this version of maestro takes. maestro <command> --help says the same in a terminal. Every command also takes -h, --help, and these: --no-color print without colours (as NO_COLOR=1 does) --server url the url of the Maestro server to talk to (default: the server the CLI kept, which it asks for the first time)
207.title: Every command

208.body:
Build a container image from a repository on one of your forges. maestro build <repo> [flags] Builds a container image from the Dockerfile, or Containerfile, at the root of a repository. When the repository's maestro.toml names another one with dockerfile = "path/to/Dockerfile", it builds from that one. Either way, the build's context is the root of the repository. <repo> is a name, owner/name or URL. The CLI uses the forge that has it, and when several of your forges have it, you pick one with --forge. A public repository on GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg needs no forge and no token: pass its full URL. The build gets a number. maestro run <build> runs its image, and maestro builds shows the builds you have. With --run, it starts a run as soon as the image is built. --watch does the same, then follows the run, not the build, until the run is over. To try a change without pushing it, send your own maestro.toml (-c), the generator it names (-g) or the Dockerfile (-f) from your computer. The server builds the repository with them in place of its own. Your files can have any name. A change to maestro.toml or the generator alone needs no new build: send the files to maestro run instead, which runs the image you have. Examples: maestro build my-app
maestro build some-org/my-app --ref v1.2.0
maestro build https://github.com/some-org/public-app
maestro build my-app --watch
maestro build my-app -c bench.toml -g genvrs.py -f Dockerfile
build=$(maestro build my-app -q) Flags: -c, --config file a file on your computer to build with as maestro.toml, in place of the repository's -f, --dockerfile file a file on your computer to build from as the Dockerfile, in place of the repository's --forge name the name of the forge to use, as maestro forges list shows it -g, --generator script a generator script on your computer, in place of the one maestro.toml names -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the build (and its run, with --run) as JSON, and nothing else on standard output -q, --quiet print only the number of the build (and its run, with --run), and nothing else on standard output --ref ref build this ref, a branch, tag or commit (default: the repository's default branch) --run start a run once the image is built -w, --watch start a run once the image is built, as --run does, and follow it until it is over
208.title: maestro build

209.body: List your builds and remove their images. maestro builds [flags] Also: image. Flags: --json print the builds as JSON Commands: maestro builds list : List your builds, and whether each still has its image maestro builds rm : Remove the image a build made maestro builds run : Run a build's image on the machines, as maestro run does
209.title: maestro builds

21.body: Every build runs every step of the Dockerfile again. Maestro keeps no layers from earlier builds, so installing dependencies takes the same time each time. A build that runs longer than the server allows, 30 minutes unless the administrator changed it, fails. Changing only the parameters doesn't need a build. maestro run <build> -c maestro.toml runs an image you already have on other lines, as Trying a change without pushing it explains.
21.breadcrumbs: The minimum: a Dockerfile » How long a build takes
21.title: How long a build takes

210.body: List your builds, and whether each still has its image. maestro builds list [flags] Lists every build of yours, newest first: the ones that worked, the ones that failed and why, and the ones still building. IMAGE is the size of the build's image, or "removed" once the image is gone. Only a build with an image can be run. BUILD is the number maestro run and maestro builds rm take. Flags: --json print the builds as JSON
210.title: maestro builds list

211.body: Remove the image a build made. maestro builds rm <build> [flags] Removes the image of a build, from the server and from the machines. You keep at most 10 images, unless your administrator set another number, and removing one frees a place for a new build. Maestro keeps the build's record and its runs, with their files. It asks first. <build> is the build's number as maestro builds list shows it, with or without #. Also: remove. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
211.title: maestro builds rm

212.body:
Run a build's image on the machines, as maestro run does. maestro builds run <build> [flags] Queues a run of a build's image. The run starts one container for each line of parameters in the repository's maestro.toml, and one for each line its generator yielded when the image was built, on the machines maestro.toml names. Without a maestro.toml, one container runs the image's own command. <build> is the build's number as maestro builds shows it, with or without #. Containers start as the machines have room. With --watch, it follows the run until the run is over, as maestro runs show <run> --watch does later, and exits with status 1 if the run failed. To try other lines without a new build, send your own maestro.toml (-c) or the generator it names (-g) from your computer. The server reads them against the repository as the build had it, and runs the build's image on the lines they make. Your files can have any name. A Dockerfile changes the image, so it takes maestro build -f. maestro help concepts says what lines are. Examples: maestro builds run 12 --watch
maestro builds run 12 -c small.toml --watch
maestro builds run 12 -g genvrs.py
run=$(maestro builds run 12 -q) && maestro runs show "$run" --watch Flags: -c, --config file a file on your computer to make the lines from as maestro.toml, in place of the build's -g, --generator script a generator script on your computer, in place of the one maestro.toml names -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the queued run as JSON, and nothing else on standard output -q, --quiet print only the number of the queued run, and nothing else on standard output -w, --watch follow the run until it is over, and exit with status 1 if it failed
212.title: maestro builds run

218.body:
Open the Maestro book, on a topic or a command. maestro docs [topic | command…] [flags] Opens the Maestro book in a browser, and prints its link. The book explains how Maestro builds, queues and runs your containers, and how to set it up. Name a topic (maestro docs queue) to open its page, or a command (maestro docs runs logs) to see what it takes. maestro carries the book, so it opens offline and without signing in. The CLI serves it from your computer only (127.0.0.1) until you press Ctrl-C, so any browser on your computer opens it whole, a sandboxed one too. Without a browser, as over SSH, it prints the link and serves the book all the same. With MAESTRO_DOCS_URL set, it opens the copy of the book at that address instead, and serves nothing itself. Also: doc. Examples: maestro docs
maestro docs toml
maestro docs runs logs
maestro docs queue --url Flags: --url only print the link, without opening a browser
218.title: maestro docs

219.body:
Write what happened to your lines over a period, as CSV. maestro export [flags] Writes a row for each line of the runs queued over a period: its run and line, whose it is, its cores and memory, the machine it ran on, its status, the scheduler settings it was assigned under, when it was submitted, assigned, started and finished, and the group its user was in when it was assigned. An administrator can measure it with orq's sim evaluate, as for a simulation: waits, slowdowns, utilization, fairness and the objective Z. Administrators can export everyone's lines with --all. Examples: maestro export --since 2026-11-01 --until 2026-11-08 > lines.csv
maestro export --since 2026-11-01 --all -o lines.csv
maestro export --since 30d -o month.csv Flags: --all everyone's lines (administrators only) -o, --output file the file to write (default: standard output) --since time start at this time: a day (2026-11-01), an RFC 3339 time, or an age such as 12h, 7d or 2w (default: a week ago) --until time end before this time, given the same ways (default: now)
219.title: maestro export

22.body: The template starts Python with -u, which turns off output buffering. Without it, Python holds back what the program prints until a buffer fills, and maestro runs logs <run> <line> -f shows nothing for a long time. In other languages, flush standard output after each line you want to see.

22.title: Printing as the program runs

220.body: Add, list and remove the git forges Maestro reads repositories from. maestro forges [flags] Lists the git forges the CLI keeps. A forge is where your repositories live: GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg, or another Forgejo or Gitea server. Maestro only reads from it. Also: forge. Flags: --json print the forges as JSON Commands: maestro forges add : Add a forge and its token maestro forges list : List your forges maestro forges rm : Remove a forge and forget its token
220.title: maestro forges

221.body:
Add a forge and its token. maestro forges add [name] [flags] Adds a forge, or replaces the one with the same name. It checks the token before it keeps it. Only a Forgejo forge takes --url. The CLI keeps the token in the system keyring. Without --store-in-file, adding a forge goes back to the keyring. With it, the CLI keeps secrets in the config file. Examples: maestro forges add
maestro forges add --kind gitlab
maestro forges add work --kind forgejo --url https://git.example.com Flags: --kind kind the kind of forge: github, forgejo, gitlab --store-in-file keep secrets in the config file from now on, instead of the system keyring --url url the Forgejo server's url (default: https://codeberg.org)
221.title: maestro forges add

222.body: List your forges. maestro forges list [flags] Flags: --json print the forges as JSON
222.title: maestro forges list

223.body: Remove a forge and forget its token. maestro forges rm <name> [flags] Also: remove. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
223.title: maestro forges rm

224.body:
List and revoke your Maestro keys. maestro keys [flags] Lists the Maestro keys you have on the server, newest first. Each maestro login issues one, on whichever computer you run it. A key is shown by its prefix, the first 10 characters, and never in full, with when it was created and when it expires. It marks the one this computer uses. A key expires 90 days after it was issued, unless your administrator set another length. Run maestro login again for a new one. Examples: maestro keys
maestro keys rm mk_Q3xv9aZ Flags: --json print the keys as JSON Commands: maestro keys rm : Revoke one of your Maestro keys
224.title: maestro keys

225.body: Revoke one of your Maestro keys. maestro keys rm <prefix> [flags] Revokes the key that starts with <prefix>, as maestro keys shows it. The key stops working at once, on every computer that holds it. It asks first. Revoke a key this way when you no longer trust a computer you signed in on. To end the key of the computer you are on, maestro logout does it and forgets the key too. Also: revoke. Examples: maestro keys rm mk_Q3xv9aZ Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
225.title: maestro keys rm

226.body: Sign the CLI in to Maestro. maestro login [flags] Prints a link to the Maestro page and a short code for you to approve there. You can open the link in any browser, on your computer or another one. With --server, it signs you in to that Maestro server, and every later command talks to it. Without --server, it uses the server the CLI has kept, and asks for one the first time. The CLI sends your key only to the server that issued it. The CLI keeps your key in the system keyring. Without --store-in-file, maestro login goes back to the keyring. If your keyring asks for a password, or you have none, pass --store-in-file to keep secrets in the config file instead. Only you can read that file. Flags: --store-in-file keep secrets in the config file from now on, instead of the system keyring
226.title: maestro login

227.body: Revoke your Maestro key and forget everything the CLI has stored. maestro logout [flags] Revokes the Maestro key on the server that issued it, then forgets the key, the server and every forge with its token on your computer. If the server can't be reached, it still forgets the key, and says that the key is still valid there. Revoke it later with maestro keys rm <prefix> from a computer that is signed in. A forge token stays valid on its forge. Revoke it there if you no longer trust this computer. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
227.title: maestro logout

228.body: List the machines containers run on, and how loaded they are. maestro machines [flags] Also: machine. Flags: --json print the machines as JSON Commands: maestro machines list : List the machines, and whether Maestro can reach them now maestro machines stats : Print how loaded the machines are, once
228.title: maestro machines

229.body: List the machines, and whether Maestro can reach them now. maestro machines list [flags] Lists the machines an administrator added on the Maestro page. maestro.toml names a machine by the name this list shows. Flags: --json print the machines as JSON
229.title: maestro machines list

23.body:
maestro.toml is an optional file at the root of the repository, beside the Dockerfile. It says how many containers a run starts and with which arguments, how much of a machine each one may use, and which files to keep. Every key is optional. A key you leave out keeps the default from the previous chapter : one container, the image's own command, 1 core, 512 MB, any machine, no files. A line runs for as long as the server lets it, a week unless your administrator set another limit. This is the template's file, with its comments removed: parameters = [ "-t 10 out.txt", "-t 20 --label 'long run' out.txt",
] outputs = ["out.txt"] Maestro reads maestro.toml when it builds the repository and keeps the result with the build, so every run of a build has the same lines. To change them, push the change and build again, or send the file with a run . The sections below add one key at a time. Each can be tried on your copy of the template: edit, push, and maestro build <your copy> --watch.
23.breadcrumbs: maestro.toml: how the image is run » maestro.toml: how the image is run
23.title: maestro.toml: how the image is run

230.body: Print how loaded the machines are, once. maestro machines stats [machine] [flags] Prints a table of every machine once: its CPU, memory, GPUs and load, the cores and memory lines take of what it has for them, with the lines waiting as +N, and its containers. With --json, it prints everything Maestro knows, for scripts. To watch the machines, use maestro top. Flags: --json print everything as JSON
230.title: maestro machines stats

231.body:
Show where lines wait, and your share of the machines. maestro queue [flags] Shows how many lines wait and run, everyone's together and yours: queued in their user's queue
heads how many of those are their user's head, in the dispatcher queue
assigned given to a machine, waiting for room on it
starting, running It also shows your share of the machines, as the scheduler weighs it when it chooses whose line goes next. A user's head is the first of their queued lines. Users are in groups, and the heads of a group's users make its dispatcher queue. Groups take turns at the machines, and in a group's turn one of its heads goes to a machine. You see your group. Administrators see every user and every group, with the number an administrator weighs a user by. When an administrator has set the most cores a user's lines may hold, it says so when your next line waits for that. It ends with how the scheduler is set up. maestro settings shows all of it. Flags: --json print the queue as JSON
231.title: maestro queue

232.body: List the repositories your forges can see. maestro repos [flags] Also: repo. Flags: --forge name the name of the forge to use, as maestro forges list shows it --json print the repositories as JSON Commands: maestro repos list : List the repositories your forge tokens can see
232.title: maestro repos

233.body: List the repositories your forge tokens can see. maestro repos list [flags] Lists one forge's repositories. The left and right arrows switch to another forge, and --forge picks the one shown first. When its output goes to a pipe, or with --json, it prints every forge's repositories once instead, or only those of --forge. Flags: --forge name the name of the forge to use, as maestro forges list shows it --json print the repositories as JSON
233.title: maestro repos list

234.body:
Run the image of one of your builds on the machines. maestro run <build> [flags] Queues a run of a build's image. The run starts one container for each line of parameters in the repository's maestro.toml, and one for each line its generator yielded when the image was built, on the machines maestro.toml names. Without a maestro.toml, one container runs the image's own command. <build> is the build's number as maestro builds shows it, with or without #. Containers start as the machines have room. With --watch, it follows the run until the run is over, as maestro runs show <run> --watch does later, and exits with status 1 if the run failed. To try other lines without a new build, send your own maestro.toml (-c) or the generator it names (-g) from your computer. The server reads them against the repository as the build had it, and runs the build's image on the lines they make. Your files can have any name. A Dockerfile changes the image, so it takes maestro build -f. maestro help concepts says what lines are. Examples: maestro run 12 --watch
maestro run 12 -c small.toml --watch
maestro run 12 -g genvrs.py
run=$(maestro run 12 -q) && maestro runs show "$run" --watch Flags: -c, --config file a file on your computer to make the lines from as maestro.toml, in place of the build's -g, --generator script a generator script on your computer, in place of the one maestro.toml names -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the queued run as JSON, and nothing else on standard output -q, --quiet print only the number of the queued run, and nothing else on standard output -w, --watch follow the run until it is over, and exit with status 1 if it failed
234.title: maestro run

235.body: List, show and download your runs. maestro runs [flags] Flags: --all everyone's runs (administrators only) -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the runs as JSON --limit n show the newest n runs, or all of them with 0 (default 20) --repo repo only the runs of this repo, as owner/name or name --status status only the runs with this status -w, --watch keep showing it as it changes Commands: maestro runs cancel : Cancel a run: drop what hasn't started and stop what has maestro runs get : Download the files kept from a run maestro runs list : List your runs maestro runs logs : Print what a line's container wrote to standard output and standard error maestro runs retry : Run some of a run's lines again, in a new run of the same build maestro runs rm : Delete a finished run and the files kept from it maestro runs show : Show each line of a run: where it ran, how it ended, what it kept
235.title: maestro runs

236.body:
Cancel a run: drop what hasn't started and stop what has. maestro runs cancel <run> [flags] Cancels a run. Its lines that haven't started end as cancelled at once. Its running lines stop soon, and Maestro keeps their logs and outputs. With --line, it cancels only the lines you name and leaves the rest. A line that is already over can't be cancelled. Examples: maestro runs cancel 31
maestro runs cancel 31 --line 2 --line 5 Flags: --line n only line n (again for more)
236.title: maestro runs cancel

237.body:
Download the files kept from a run. maestro runs get <run> [dir] [flags] Downloads every file kept from a run's containers into <dir>/<run>/<line>/, with what each container printed beside them, as stdout.log and stderr.log. <dir> is the current directory unless you give one. --line picks some lines only. Without --force, it won't download over a run already downloaded there. Examples: maestro runs get 31
maestro runs get 31 results/ --line 2 --line 5 Flags: --force download over a run already downloaded there --line n only line n (again for more)
237.title: maestro runs get

238.body: List your runs. maestro runs list [flags] Lists your runs, newest first. It shows your 20 newest, or as many as --limit says, and --limit 0 shows them all. --status (queued, running, succeeded, failed, cancelled) and --repo narrow the list, and --json prints the same runs. With --watch, it draws the list again every --interval until you press Ctrl-C. With --all, an administrator sees everyone's runs, and whose each one is. Flags: --all everyone's runs (administrators only) -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the runs as JSON --limit n show the newest n runs, or all of them with 0 (default 20) --repo repo only the runs of this repo, as owner/name or name --status status only the runs with this status -w, --watch keep showing it as it changes
238.title: maestro runs list

239.body:
Print what a line's container wrote to standard output and standard error. maestro runs logs <run> [line] [flags] Prints what a line's container wrote. What it wrote to standard output goes to your standard output, and what it wrote to standard error goes to your standard error, so you can tell the two apart or send them to different places. You can leave out the line of a run that has only one. With -f, it waits for a line that hasn't started yet, and follows what a running line prints until the line ends, as tail -f does. Once a line is over, all of its standard output comes before all of its standard error. Maestro doesn't keep how the two were interleaved as the container ran. Examples: maestro runs logs 31 2 -f
maestro runs logs 31 2 2>/dev/null # only what it printed to standard output
maestro runs logs 31 2 >/dev/null # only what it printed to standard error Flags: -f, --follow wait for the line to start, and follow what it prints until it ends --tail n only the last n lines of a line still running (default: all)
239.title: maestro runs logs

24.title: parameters

240.body:
Run some of a run's lines again, in a new run of the same build. maestro runs retry <run> [flags] Queues a new run of the same build with some of the run's lines. Each line runs with the arguments, cores, memory, environment and outputs it had, and keeps its number, so line 2 of the new run is line 2 of the old one. Without --line, it takes the lines that failed, ended in an error or were cancelled, as --failed does. With --line, it takes exactly the lines you name, whatever their status, so you can run a line that succeeded again too. A line still waiting or running can't run again until it ends. With --watch, it follows the new run until the run is over, as maestro run --watch does. Examples: maestro runs retry 31
maestro runs retry 31 --line 2 --watch Flags: --failed the lines that failed, ended in an error or were cancelled (the default) -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the queued run as JSON, and nothing else on standard output --line n line n (again for more) -q, --quiet print only the number of the queued run, and nothing else on standard output -w, --watch follow the new run until it is over, and exit with status 1 if it failed
240.title: maestro runs retry

241.body: Delete a finished run and the files kept from it. maestro runs rm <run> [flags] Also: remove. Flags: -y, --yes don't ask first
241.title: maestro runs rm

242.body: Show each line of a run: where it ran, how it ended, what it kept. maestro runs show [run] [flags] Shows each line of a run: where it ran, how it ended and what it kept. Without a run, it shows your newest. With --watch, it draws the run again every --interval until the run is over or you press Ctrl-C, and exits with status 1 if the run failed. Flags: --failed only the lines that failed, ended in an error or were cancelled -n, --interval duration how often to redraw with --watch, at least 1s (default 2s) --json print the run as JSON -w, --watch keep showing it as it changes, and exit with status 1 if the run failed
242.title: maestro runs show

243.body: Show the server's settings: the limits on each user and how lines are scheduled. maestro settings [flags] Shows how many images each user may keep and how many cores each user's lines may hold, and how the scheduler chooses whose line goes next and where: the policy of each of the three queues, the score's weights and how a user's share of the machines is measured. An administrator changes them on the Maestro page. Flags: --json print the settings as JSON
243.title: maestro settings

244.body: Watch how loaded the machines are, like top. maestro top [machine] [flags] Shows one row for each machine: its CPU, memory, GPUs and load. Under CORES, 6/14 +3 means lines use 6 of the 14 cores the machine has for them and 3 more lines wait. The rows refresh every 2 seconds, or as often as -n says. Press Enter on a machine to see its cores, memory, disks, network and GPUs, and the containers on it with whose each one is. Name a machine to open it straight away. Anyone signed in sees the machines and their own containers. Administrators also see every container, and the server Maestro runs on, as "orq". However many windows are open, Maestro reads each machine at most once every 2 seconds, and everyone watching shares that reading. Flags: -n, --interval duration how often to redraw, at least 1s (default 2s)
244.title: maestro top

245.body:
Show how much your lines have used. maestro usage [flags] Shows the core-hours and memory GB-hours your lines used over the last 30 days, or as many as --days says. A line counts when it ends. If an administrator set the scheduler up so, what you used counts against you when it chooses whose line goes next, and older usage counts less. Administrators see everyone's usage, or one user's with --user, by their number or email. Examples: maestro usage --daily --days 7
maestro usage --user ana@example.org Flags: --daily a row for each day --days n look back n days (default 30) --json print the usage as JSON, a day at a time --user user one user's usage, by their number or email (administrators only)
245.title: maestro usage

246.body: maestro.toml sits at the root of the repository. The file and every key in it are optional. maestro.toml: how the image is run introduces the keys one at a time, and this page is the lookup table.

247.body: Key Type Default What it sets parameters List of strings One line that runs the image's own CMD The lines of a run. Each string becomes the arguments of one container. generator String None A Python script in the repository whose genvrs function yields more lines outputs List of strings None, so only the logs are kept The files and directories to keep from each container outputs_layout "per-line" or "shared" "per-line" Whether each line's outputs go in a directory of their own or all into one tree for the run outputs_every Duration, such as "30m" None, so outputs are copied only when a line ends How often a running line's logs and outputs are copied out cpus Whole number 1 The cores each container can use, and the cores a machine must have free to start it memory Whole number, in MB 512 The memory each container can use, and the memory a machine must have free to start it env Table of strings None Environment variables set in every container retries Whole number 0 How many times a line that loses its machine goes back to the queue time Duration, such as "90m" or "2h" The server's limit, a week unless your administrator set another The longest each line may run before Maestro stops it machines List of strings Any machine The only machines the lines can run on dockerfile String Containerfile at the root, or else Dockerfile The file the image is built from

249.body: Maestro splits each line of parameters, and each string a generator yields, at spaces and tabs. No shell is involved. Written Meaning 'two words' One argument. Everything inside single quotes is taken as written. "two words" One argument. Inside double quotes, a backslash keeps the next character as written, so \" is a quote. two\ words One argument. A backslash keeps the next character as written. $HOME, *, ~ Passed to the program as typed, because no shell expands them A line with a quote left open, or one that ends in a backslash, is an error.

25.body: outputs = ["out.txt", "results/", "plots/summary.png"] These are the files Maestro copies out of each container when it ends, whether the program succeeded or failed. Each path is a path inside the container. A relative one starts at the image's WORKDIR, which is /work in the template. A directory is kept with everything in it. A file the program didn't write is listed as missing, and the line's status doesn't change because of it. What the container prints is always kept, as stdout.log and stderr.log, whatever outputs says. What a line leaves behind shows where everything ends up.

MAESTRO_ORQ_ADDR :8081 Where orq listens. The compose file uses :3005. 26.body:
cpus = 4 # whole cores; default 1
memory = 8192 # MB; default 512 These two numbers do two jobs. They limit the container. It can use the processor time of cpus cores and no more. If it takes more memory than memory, the kernel kills it, and the line ends failed, usually with exit code 137. They also decide where and when the line starts. A machine starts a line only when that many cores and that much memory are free on it. A smaller request fits on more machines and starts sooner. Maestro refuses a run when one of its lines would not fit on any machine it may use, even an empty one: line 3 asks for 64 cpus and 512 MB, which no machine it may use has for lines even with nothing else on it (see `maestro machines list`) maestro machines shows what each machine has. A program doesn't learn its limit by counting the machine's cores, so read how many threads to start before giving a multithreaded program more than one core.

288.body: Word Meaning More Repo A git repository of yours on GitHub, GitLab, Codeberg, or another Forgejo or Gitea server. It holds your program and a Dockerfile, and usually a maestro.toml that says how to run the image. Your own copy of the template Forge The place a repository lives, as Maestro reaches it: the forge's API and a read-only token of yours. The CLI keeps the token and sends it to the server when the server needs to clone. A forge never signs anyone in. Git forges Build The result of maestro build <repo>, which clones a repository at one commit and builds a container image from it. A build has a number, written #12. The build also reads maestro.toml and computes the lines, so every run of a build has the same lines. Builds and images Image What a build makes: your program and everything it needs, ready to start as a container. You keep 10 at a time unless your administrator set another number. When a new build needs room, the image you ran least recently is removed. How many images you keep Run The result of maestro run <build>, which runs a build's image on the machines. A run has a number of its own, written run 31. Build numbers and run numbers count separately. Runs and lines Line One container of a run. maestro.toml lists lines of parameters and can name a generator that computes more. A run starts one container for each line, with the line's words in place of the image's CMD. Without a maestro.toml, a run is one line that runs the image's own command. A run has at most 5000 lines. parameters Retry A run that maestro runs retry made from some lines of an earlier run of the same build. Each line keeps its number, so a retry's lines can skip numbers. Running lines again Generator A Python script in the repository whose genvrs function yields lines. Generating lines with Python Outputs The files maestro.toml names, copied out of each container when it ends. They are kept beside what the container printed, stdout.log and stderr.log. maestro runs get downloads all of it. What a line leaves behind Machine A computer whose Podman runs the containers. Maestro reaches it over SSH. A line runs on one machine, the first allowed one that has room for its cores and memory. Watching the machines Maestro key What the CLI signs in with. maestro login has the server issue one for your computer, and the CLI sends it with every command. A key is shown by its prefix, its first 10 characters, such as mk_Q3xv9aZ. It expires 90 days after it was issued, unless your administrator set another length. maestro keys rm revokes one, maestro logout revokes the one it holds, and an administrator can revoke all of a user's. A revoked key stops working at once. Signing in Group A set of users. Groups take turns at the machines, so a lab of ten doesn't crowd out a lab of two. Everyone is in one group until an administrator makes more. Groups
