288.title: The things you work with

289.body: A line waits in three queues before it runs: its user's queue, its group's dispatcher queue as its user's head, and a machine's queue. Status The line is queued In its user's queue. The first of a user's queued lines is their head, which waits in the dispatcher queue for a machine. assigned Given to a machine, and waiting for room on it while its image is copied there starting, running In a container on the machine It then ends in one of four ways. Status What happened succeeded The program exited with 0. failed The program exited with another code. error The line couldn't run, for a reason on Maestro's side and outside your program. A line that runs longer than the server allows is stopped and ends as error too. cancelled It or its run was cancelled before it ended. The queue explains the three queues, and How a line ends the endings.

291.body: Word Meaning User queue A user's queued lines, in the order the user policy gives them Head The first line of a user's queue, the one their group's dispatcher queue holds for them Dispatcher queue The heads of a group's users. In the group's turn, the dispatcher policy gives one of them a machine. Machine queue The lines assigned to a machine that wait for room on it, at most depth of them Policy The rule that picks who leaves one of the three queues, such as fifo or pq Score The number pq ranks lines by, built from a line's cores, memory and waiting time and its user's share Share How much of the machines a user holds or has used, as the chosen measure counts it Ceiling The most cores a user's lines assigned, starting and running may hold together, user_max_cpus. A head that would take its user over it waits. 0 means no ceiling. The queue describes the queues, and Policies and the score the policies, the score and the share.

31.body: outputs_layout = "shared" # default: "per-line" With per-line, each line's outputs go in a directory of its own, <run>/<line>/<path>. Two lines can both write out.txt and both files are kept. With shared, every line's outputs go into one tree for the whole run, <run>/shared/<path>. This suits a program whose lines each fill in part of one results directory, such as results/<instance>/<seed>.json. When two lines write the same path, the one Maestro collects last overwrites the other, so give each line paths of its own. Logs stay separate for each line in both layouts.

32.body: outputs_every = "30m" # default: only when the line ends This is how often Maestro copies a line's logs and outputs out of its container while it runs. Each copy takes the place of the one before, in the same directory and within the same limit. If the line then loses its machine, it keeps the last copy, and its note says when that copy was taken. It must be at least "10m". It suits a line that runs for days and writes results as it goes. A line that ends within hours doesn't need it. The copy holds what the program had written when Maestro took it, so a file it was in the middle of writing can be cut short. A program that writes its results to a new file and then renames it over the old one leaves a whole file to copy.

36.body: Writing lines by hand works for a few of them. A grid of parameters, or one line for each instance file, is easier to compute. A generator is a Python script in the repository that defines a function called genvrs. Every string the function yields becomes one line, split into words the same way a line of parameters is.

37.body: The template already has one, genvrs.py: def genvrs(): for seconds in (10, 20, 30): yield f"-t {seconds} out.txt" Its maestro.toml has the line that enables it commented out. Remove the #: generator = "genvrs.py" Push and build. The build log now counts five containers: Read maestro.toml: 5 lines (3 from genvrs.py) on any machine, with 1 core and 512 MB each, keeping out.txt. The two lines of parameters come first, then the three the generator yielded. If you delete parameters, the generator's lines are the whole run.

38.body:
import itertools
from collections.abc import Generator def genvrs() -> Generator[str]: for t, seed in itertools.product([10, 20, 30], range(3)): yield f"-t {t} --seed {seed} out.txt" This yields nine lines, from -t 10 --seed 0 out.txt to -t 30 --seed 2 out.txt.

40.body: By default every generated line runs with the cpus, memory, env, outputs, time and retries of maestro.toml. To change them for some lines, define a class called Config above genvrs and assign to its attributes before yielding. Each line runs with what the class holds at the moment the line is yielded. class Config: outputs: list[str] | None = None # None: what maestro.toml says cpus: int | None = 4 # 4 cores, whatever maestro.toml says memory: int | None = None env: dict[str, str] | None = None time: str | None = None retries: int | None = None def genvrs() -> Generator[str]: yield "-t 10 small" # 4 cores, maestro.toml's memory Config.memory = 4096 for seed in range(3): Config.env = {"SEED": str(seed)} yield "-t 10 large" # 4 cores, 4096 MB, SEED 0, 1 and 2 Config.memory = None yield "-t 10 medium" # 4 cores, maestro.toml's memory again None means "what maestro.toml says, or the default if it says nothing". The class may hold only these six attributes. machines is the same for every line and is set in maestro.toml.
40.breadcrumbs: Generating lines with Python » Lines that need different settings
40.title: Lines that need different settings

41.body: Maestro runs the script once, during the build, and the build keeps the lines it yielded. Every run of that build has the same lines. A script that draws random numbers should seed them (random.Random(2026)), so that building the same commit twice gives the same lines. The script runs inside the Maestro server, in a sandbox, and not in your image. The sandbox is a Python 3.14 with the standard library and nothing else. That has consequences: Packages from requirements.txt aren't there, and neither is anything that needs compiling, such as numpy. The script can read the repository's files and import its other modules. It can't write files. It has no network and no environment variables. It gets 256 MB of memory and 30 seconds. What the script prints goes to the build log, which makes print a good way to check what it computed.

MAESTRO_OUTPUTS The line's outputs, one path on each text line

46.body:
A limit on cores doesn't change how many cores a program sees. nproc, os.cpu_count() and most libraries still report every core of the machine. A program that starts one thread for each core it sees starts far more threads than it has cores to run them on, and gets slower. Read MAESTRO_CPUS and start that many. The template's knapsack branch does it for its solver: import os # As many threads as the container has cores; outside Maestro, 0 lets the
# solver choose.
model.threads = int(os.environ.get("MAESTRO_CPUS", "0")) Most solvers have an option for this, such as Gurobi's Threads, CPLEX's threads and num_workers in OR-Tools. Programs built on OpenMP read OMP_NUM_THREADS, which a small start script can set from MAESTRO_CPUS before it starts the program.

47.body: When a container takes more memory than its memory, the kernel kills it. The line ends failed, usually with exit code 137. Ask for what the program needs at its largest, plus some room. A smaller request starts sooner, but a line that is killed has to run again from the start.

48.body: Some machines can't enforce the limit on cores. This happens when Podman runs without root and the system doesn't give it the cpu cgroup controller, which is the default on Ubuntu 22.04. On such a machine a line still counts as using its cpus, and MAESTRO_CPUS is still set, but a program that starts more threads does take more cores and slows the lines beside it. An administrator can fix the machine once, as Adding machines describes.

Start it with -u, set PYTHONUNBUFFERED=1 in the image, or print with flush=True. Maestro keeps up to 1 GB of logs and outputs for each line, unless your administrator set another limit. It drops the rest and notes that on the line.

51.body:
Committing and pushing for every experiment with maestro.toml gets slow. maestro build and maestro run can take three files from your computer and use them in place of the repository's: Flag Replaces -c <file> maestro.toml at the root of the repository -g <file> The generator that maestro.toml names. When it names none, the script is added at the root under its own name and used. -f <file> The Dockerfile that maestro.toml names, or else Dockerfile at the root. Only maestro build takes it. The file on your computer can have any name. maestro build my-app -c bench.toml -g genvrs.py -f Dockerfile # a new image
maestro run 81 -c small.toml --watch # build #81's image, other lines

52.body: maestro run <build> -c or -g doesn't build anything. The server clones the repository again at the commit the build was made from, puts your files over the clone, runs the generator there, and starts the build's image on the lines that result. It takes seconds, because no image is built. Use it to try other parameters, other cpus and memory, other machines or another seed. For a private repository the CLI sends the forge token it has, so the server can clone. A run doesn't take -f, and it ignores a dockerfile key in the maestro.toml you send, because it builds no image.

52.title: With a run: other lines, same image

53.body: maestro build puts your files over its clone before it reads anything, so the image is built with them. Use it when the Dockerfile changes. A change to the program itself still has to be pushed. These flags replace only the three files above.

54.body: The lines of such a build or run don't come from the commit alone, so maestro builds and maestro runs show say which files you sent. What you send is checked the way a build checks the repository's files, and an invalid file fails the build or refuses the run. A file can be at most 1 MiB.

Two other branches of the same repository use more of what the previous chapters covered. --ref builds a branch: maestro build https://github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template --ref knapsack Both branches name the machines of the lab they were written for in machines. On another Maestro, a run of them is refused because those machines don't exist. Fork the repository and remove the machines line, or start the run with a maestro.toml of your own: maestro run <build> -c my.toml.

56.body: This branch solves knapsack problems with the mip solver, one container for each instance and capacity. File What it shows maestro.toml Two lines of parameters, a generator, cpus, memory, an env variable and one output, solution.json genvrs.py Reads every file in instances/ and yields three lines for each, with the capacity scaled by 0.25, 0.5 and 2 main.py Solves one instance, with as many solver threads as MAESTRO_CPUS says requirements.txt The solver, installed by the Dockerfile The generator gives larger instances more than the rest. An instance with more than 30 items gets 1024 MB through Config.memory and a time limit of 60 seconds, where a small one keeps maestro.toml's 512 MB and gets 10 seconds. It also prints one line for each instance, which shows up in the build log. With three instance files, a run has eleven lines: two from parameters and nine from the generator.

57.body:
This branch is a stress test of the queue. Its containers do no useful work. Each one sleeps, keeps its cores busy, fills part of its memory, or does both, for between ten seconds and four minutes, and writes a report.json with what it used. maestro.toml lists four lines and genvrs.py adds 996, which makes 1000. The generator draws each line's size from ten shapes, from 1 core and 64 MB up to 10 cores and 10 GB, with a fixed seed so that every build yields the same lines. One line in ten also keeps a samples.csv, and every hundredth line exits with code 3 on purpose, so the run has failed lines to look at. It is a good run to have going while you read The queue : maestro queue # how many lines wait in each queue
maestro top # each machine as it fills

63.body: Maestro has no passwords of its own. It signs you in through your lab's identity provider, with the account you use for the lab's other services.
63.title: Signing in

64.body: Open the Maestro page and press the sign-in button. The identity provider asks for your account, and sends you back signed in. A session lasts 12 hours unless your administrator set another length. Signing out of Maestro ends the Maestro session and leaves you signed in at the identity provider. Signing out there doesn't end a Maestro session that is already open.
64.title: In the browser

65.body: maestro login maestro login prints a link to the Maestro page and a short code. Open the link, sign in there if the page asks, and approve the code. The CLI then receives a key of its own and uses it for every command. A key expires 90 days after it was issued, unless your administrator set another length. After that, commands say "this Maestro key expired; run maestro login", and maestro login gives you a new one. The CLI doesn't open the link for you. You can open it in a browser on another computer, which is how you sign in on a computer you reach over SSH.
65.title: In the terminal

66.body: The CLI stores the key in your system's keyring. On a computer without a keyring, or one whose keyring asks for a password each time, sign in with: maestro login --store-in-file The key then goes into the CLI's config file, which only your user can read.
66.breadcrumbs: Signing in » Where the key is kept
66.title: Where the key is kept

67.body: The CLI has no built-in server. The first time a command needs one, maestro asks for its address and keeps it. An address without a scheme gets https://. A script has no terminal to answer at, so there the command stops and tells you to pass --server <url>, set MAESTRO_ORQ_URL, or run maestro login --server <url> once. To use another Maestro, sign in to it: maestro login --server https://maestro.example.org Every later command talks to that server. For one command only, pass --server, or set MAESTRO_ORQ_URL. The flag wins over the variable, and the variable wins over the server the CLI kept. The CLI stores the key together with the server that issued it and sends it nowhere else. If you point a command at a different server, the CLI tells you to sign in there. maestro with no arguments shows who is signed in, on which server, and on which forges.
67.breadcrumbs: Signing in » Which server the CLI talks to
67.title: Which server the CLI talks to

68.body: Each maestro login issues a new Maestro key, for the computer you run it on. To see the keys you have: maestro keys It lists each key by its prefix, the first 10 characters, with when it was created and when it expires. It marks the key this computer uses. If you no longer trust a computer you signed in on, revoke its key from another one: maestro keys rm mk_Q3xv9aZ The key stops working at once, on every computer that holds it. The command asks first. With --yes it doesn't ask. An administrator can revoke every key of a user, from Admin › Groups on the Maestro page.
68.title: Your keys

69.body: maestro logout This revokes the key on the server that issued it. Then it removes the key, the server address and every forge token from this computer. If the server can't be reached, maestro logout still forgets the key, and says that the key is still valid on the server. Revoke it later with maestro keys rm from a computer that is signed in. maestro logout changes nothing on the forges, so revoke a token there if you no longer trust the computer it was on.
69.title: Signing out

maestro build https://github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template --watch This command clones the repository on the server, builds a container image from its Dockerfile, starts a run of that image, and follows the run until it is over. The build log streams to your terminal. These are the lines to look for in it: Building github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main...
Cloning github.com/gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main...
Read maestro.toml: 2 lines on any machine, with 1 core and 512 MB each, keeping out.txt.
STEP 1/7: FROM docker.io/library/python:3.12-slim
…
Build #12 succeeded: 5d0c3a9f2e41…
Queued run 31 of build #12: 2 line(s) on any machine.

The template's maestro.toml lists two sets of parameters, so the run has two containers. Maestro calls each one a line. After the build, --watch draws the run and redraws it every two seconds: Run 31 of gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main (build #12): running, on any machine

2 -t 20 --label 'long run' out.txt Q2 assigned - The numbers and machine names will be your server's. A line's status goes from queued to assigned while it waits, then running, then succeeded. The queue explains the waiting ones. The template's program sleeps for the number of seconds after -t, so the run takes under a minute once its lines start. The command returns when both lines have ended: Run 31 of gustaleitcor/maestro-template@main (build #12): succeeded, on any machine
2 line(s): 2 succeeded LINE PARAMETERS MACHINE STATUS FILES
1 -t 10 out.txt Q1 succeeded out.txt
2 -t 20 --label 'long run' out.txt Q2 succeeded out.txt

70.body:
A forge is the place your repositories live, such as GitHub or Codeberg. Maestro needs a forge only to read private repositories, and to let you name a repository without typing its whole address. A public repository on GitHub, GitLab or Codeberg builds from its address with no forge at all. To Maestro, a forge is the address of its API and a read-only token of yours. The CLI keeps the token on your computer and sends it to the server with each build that needs it. Maestro uses it to list and clone repositories. A forge never signs you in to Maestro. maestro forges add # add one: asks for the kind and the token
maestro forges # the forges you have
maestro repos # the repositories they can see
maestro forges rm <name> # forget one
70.title: Git forges

71.body: Kind Where Token to create github github.com A classic token with the repo scope forgejo Codeberg, or any Forgejo or Gitea server with --url Repository: Read and User: Read, everything else at No access gitlab gitlab.com, nested groups included The read_api and read_repository scopes maestro forges add tells you how to create the token. For GitHub and GitLab it prints a link that fills in the form. It checks the token before keeping it. On GitHub, use a classic token. A fine-grained token reaches the repositories of one owner only, so it can't read a private repository that belongs to someone else and that you collaborate on. GitHub and GitLab tokens expire after 30 days unless you choose otherwise when you create them. When one expires, run maestro forges add with the same name to replace it.

82.body:
A build turns one commit of a repository into a container image. Runs start from builds, so a build comes first. maestro build my-app # build the default branch
maestro build my-app --ref v1.2.0 # a branch, a tag or a commit
maestro build my-app --run # build, then start a run
maestro build my-app --watch # build, start a run, follow it to the end
maestro builds # the builds you have
maestro builds rm 12 # remove a build's image

83.body: The server clones the repository at the commit you asked for. It reads maestro.toml and runs the generator , if there is one. The lines that result are stored with the build. It builds the image from the Dockerfile. The build log streams to your terminal while this happens. Ctrl-C stops the build on the server too. When a build fails, the last lines of the log say why. The usual causes are a step of the Dockerfile, an invalid maestro.toml, and a generator that raised an exception. A finished build has a number, written #12. maestro run 12 starts a run of its image. You can have 2 builds running at once, unless your administrator set another number. Maestro refuses a third with "you already have 2 builds running; wait for one to end".

The first time one of its lines is given to a machine, Maestro copies the image there, compressed on the way, and the line stays assigned until the copy is done. The image then stays on that machine, so later runs of the same build start without the copy. A smaller image copies faster. A -slim base image and a .dockerignore that leaves out what the program doesn't use both help.

9.body: Maestro cloned the repository and built an image from its Dockerfile. That is build #12. It read maestro.toml, which lists two lines of parameters and one file to keep. --watch started run 31 of that build, with one container for each line. Each container ran the image's program with its line as arguments, on a machine that had a free core and 512 MB. When a container ended, Maestro kept its output and out.txt, then removed the container. A build and a run have separate numbers. maestro run 12 starts another run of the same image without building again, and maestro runs lists the runs you have.

90.body: --watch redraws the output in place every 2 seconds, or as often as --interval says. It works on maestro run, maestro runs show and maestro runs list. maestro runs show <run> --watch returns when the run is over. It says how the run ended and exits with status 1 if the run failed or was cancelled, so a script can wait on it. Ctrl-C stops the watching and leaves the run alone. When the output goes to a pipe, --watch prints a new copy only when something changed.
90.breadcrumbs: Runs and lines » Following a run
90.title: Following a run

91.body: maestro runs logs <run> <line> prints what the line wrote to standard output on your standard output, and what it wrote to standard error on your standard error. Redirect one away to read the other: maestro runs logs 31 2 2>/dev/null # standard output only A run with a single line doesn't need the line number. -f follows the line the way tail -f follows a file. It waits for a line that hasn't started, prints what a running line prints as it comes, and returns when the line ends. A server older than -f can't follow. The CLI then prints what the line had printed so far and says so. For a line that has ended, all of its standard output comes before all of its standard error. Maestro stores the two apart and doesn't record how they were interleaved.
91.title: Reading logs

92.body: maestro runs get <run> downloads every line's outputs and logs into a directory named after the run. What a line leaves behind describes the layout. --line picks lines, a second argument picks the directory, and --force downloads over a run that is already there.
92.title: Downloading

93.body:
maestro runs retry <run> queues a new run of the same build with some of the run's lines. Each line runs with the arguments, cores, memory, environment and outputs it had. It keeps its number too, so line 2 of the new run is line 2 of the old one, and the new run's lines can skip numbers. maestro runs retry 33 # the lines that didn't succeed
maestro runs retry 33 --line 2 --watch # line 2, whatever its status Without --line, it takes the lines that failed, ended in an error or were cancelled, as --failed does. With --line, again for more, it takes exactly the lines you name, including one that succeeded. A line still waiting or running can't run again, and the command says which status it has. Like maestro run, it takes --watch, -q and --json. The new run needs the build's image. When the image is gone, build the commit again with maestro build. On the Maestro page, a line's details have a "Run again" button that does the same for that one line.
93.breadcrumbs: Runs and lines » Running lines again
93.title: Running lines again

94.body: maestro runs cancel <run> drops the lines that haven't started and stops the ones that are running. Lines that had already ended keep their status. With --line, again for more, it cancels only the lines you name and leaves the rest of the run going. A line still waiting ends as cancelled at once. A running line stops soon, and Maestro keeps its logs and outputs. A line that is already over can't be cancelled, and the command says how it ended. A run whose lines you cancelled this way ends as its other lines do, so it can still end succeeded. On the Maestro page, a line's details have a "Cancel" button that does the same for that line. maestro runs rm <run> deletes the run with all its logs and files. It asks first.
94.breadcrumbs: Runs and lines » Cancelling and deleting
94.title: Cancelling and deleting

95.body: Status What happened succeeded The program exited with 0. failed The program exited with another code, or the kernel killed it for using more memory than the line asked for. error The line couldn't run. Most often it couldn't start on its machine, or the machine restarted while it ran and the container was lost. cancelled You cancelled the line or its run before the line ended. A line runs for at most a week, unless your administrator set another length. When a line runs longer, Maestro stops it, keeps its logs and outputs, and ends it as error with the note "stopped after 168 hours, the longest a line may run on this server". A line can ask for less with time in maestro.toml. Past that time, Maestro stops it the same way, with the note "stopped after 2h, the time this line asked for". Any other error comes from the system and says nothing about your program. The Maestro page shows such lines in amber with the reason, and maestro runs retry runs them again. A line whose machine restarts or is removed while it runs, or whose container disappears, ends as error too. With retries in maestro.toml, it goes back to queued instead, as many times as retries says, and starts again from the beginning. Its details on the Maestro page say how many attempts it took. A line that exits with a code, that you cancel, or that runs out of time never goes back. A machine that stops answering doesn't turn its waiting lines into errors. Maestro moves them back to queued so another machine can take them. Lines already running on that machine are left alone and checked again when it returns.

95.title: How a line ends

96.body: When a container ends, Maestro keeps what it printed and the files that outputs names, then removes the container. Everything else the program wrote inside it is gone.

96.title: What a line leaves behind

97.body: With outputs_every , Maestro also copies the logs and outputs of a running line that often, into the same place. Each copy takes the place of the one before, and the copy taken when the line ends takes the place of the last. A line that loses its machine keeps the last copy, and its note says when it was taken: q7 restarted while this line ran there, and its container was lost; its logs and outputs are those copied at 2026-11-17 14:30 UTC Without outputs_every, a line that loses its machine keeps nothing.

98.body:
maestro runs get <run> downloads a run into a directory named after it, with one directory for each line: 31/
├── 1/
│ ├── report.json
│ ├── stderr.log
│ └── stdout.log
├── 2/
│ └── …
└── shared/ (with outputs_layout = "shared") └── results/… A run downloaded from the Maestro page comes as a zip with the same layout.

98.title: The layout of a download

99.body: Maestro keeps standard output and standard error apart, as stdout.log and stderr.log in the line's directory. Both files exist even when the program printed nothing to one of them. The two names are reserved. If outputs lists a file called stdout.log or stderr.log, Maestro keeps the log and drops the program's file. Runs made before Maestro kept the two streams apart have both in one file, <line>.log, beside the line's directory. Maestro still reads those.
